title: Sikkim on a budget: what it really costs
meta_description: What a Sikkim trip costs in 2026: daily budgets by tier, shared jeep and permit-tour prices, homestay rates, food costs and six ways to spend less.
summary: A saver trip in Sikkim runs about ₹2,000–3,500 a day per person if you use homestays and shared jeeps, rising to ₹7,000–12,000 for comfort and ₹25,000–50,000 for signature. Permits and North Sikkim transport are the big variables. All prices here are indicative 2026.

sections.heading: Daily budgets by tier
paras: Sikkim is cheaper than most Himalayan regions in the west, but the cost curve bends sharply once you enter permit country. Below Mangan and around Gangtok, Pelling and Yuksom you can move on your own with shared jeeps and local taxis. Above it, in Lachung, Lachen, Gurudongmar, Zuluk and Tsomgo, you generally need a registered agent and a vehicle, and prices jump.

The ranges below are per person per day, twin sharing, and are indicative for 2026. They cover a bed, food and local transport, not your trip to Siliguri or Bagdogra. Season matters: April–May and October–November are peak, and the same room can cost 30–50 percent more than in January or July. Check current prices before you travel.

A useful rule of thumb is to price the trip in two parts. First, the fixed part: your return travel to Bagdogra or New Jalpaiguri, which depends on where you start. Second, the daily part, which depends on tier and season. A week in Gangtok, Pelling and Yuksom on a saver budget, for example, comes to roughly ₹14,000–25,000 for the days, plus your arrival, while the same week with a private car and good hotels reaches ₹50,000–85,000 per person. We build every trip on our site in these three tiers so you can compare.

sections.heading: Getting around and what a permit tour costs
paras: Shared jeeps are the backbone of Sikkim's transport. They leave from fixed stands in Gangtok, Siliguri, Jorethang, Pelling and other towns, and go when full, so mornings are best. Fares on the main legs are low compared with a private taxi, but they change; ask the driver or stand office before you board.

North Sikkim and Tsomgo change the maths. A shared seat to Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok costs roughly ₹800–1,500, and a private vehicle costs ₹3,500–5,500, rising to ₹6,000–9,000 if Nathu La is added. A private jeep for Lachung and Yumthang costs roughly ₹9,000–15,000 depending on season, and Lachen with Gurudongmar usually costs more. Agents quote a package that includes permits; check current status before you travel.

One more point on transport. Private cars registered outside Sikkim are generally not allowed beyond the check posts on the Tsomgo and North Sikkim roads, so self-drive savings are not available there. Local registered taxis are required, and the agent usually arranges the permit. Ask for the full price, including permit processing and any union charges, before you pay a deposit, and keep a receipt.

sections.heading: Where you sleep and what you pay
paras: Homestays are the heart of saver travel in Sikkim. In Lachung, Yuksom and Zuluk, family homes take guests with dinner and breakfast included, usually for ₹1,500–3,000 per person a night, and the money stays in the village. Bathrooms may be shared and hot water comes in buckets in winter, but the food is home-cooked and the kitchen stove is the warm room.

In towns, a simple Gangtok or Pelling guesthouse costs ₹1,200–3,000 a room in low season. Mid-range hotels, such as Hotel Tibet or Netuk House in Gangtok and The Chumbi Mountain Retreat in Pelling, cost ₹4,000–11,000 a night for a double. The Elgin Nor-Khill and Mayfair Spa Resort in Gangtok and The Elgin Mount Pandim in Pelling sit at ₹12,000–30,000 for a double. Check current status before you travel; rates move with season and festival dates.

If you want a hotel for one night in a town and a homestay for the rest, that mix keeps costs down without losing comfort. Gangtok's central guesthouses sell out around festivals and long weekends, so book early for those dates and leave the rest flexible.

sections.heading: What you spend on food
paras: Food is good value. A plate of momos in Gangtok costs roughly ₹80–200, a bowl of thukpa ₹120–250, and a simple thali ₹150–350. Hotel restaurants are two or three times that. Homestays include dinner and breakfast, so your main extra spend is lunch on the road, which many agencies include on permit tours.

Sikkim has strict rules on plastic bags and a growing campaign against single-use plastic. Carry a refillable bottle and a cloth bag to avoid small fines and extra costs. Tea, local millet beer called tongba, and fresh cheese called churpi are cheap and worth trying, but ask the price first at tourist stalls.

sections.heading: Six ways to spend less without losing the trip
paras: Cost savings come from planning, not from skipping the sights. We suggest:
list: Travel in April–May or October–November only if your dates are fixed; January, February, July and August are cheaper, though cold or wet.
Take shared seats on permit tours, and ask the agency to match you with other travellers.
Choose homestays in Lachung, Yuksom and Zuluk, which include dinner and breakfast.
Book permit-tour packages in Gangtok, not online from far away, and compare two or three registered agents.
Pre-book nothing for Siliguri–Gangtok; shared jeeps leave from stands and cost far less than a taxi.
Use two or three bases and day trips, rather than moving every night.

sections.heading: What costs more than you expect
paras: Three things catch first-time visitors. First, permit tours: a Lachung day trip looks cheap until you add a private jeep and the cost of the Lachen leg. Second, peak-season hotel rates in Gangtok and Pelling during Durga Puja, Diwali and the Christmas–New Year weeks. Third, cash: ATMs in Lachung, Lachen and Yuksom are few or empty, so withdraw in Gangtok.

Also plan for time. A delay by landslide can force an extra night, and a missed flight costs more than the room. Keep a buffer day before any onward flight or train, and carry a small reserve of cash. Travel insurance that covers high-altitude trekking, if you plan Goecha La, is also worth the price.

sections.heading: A sample week with numbers
paras: To make this concrete, here is how a seven-night saver trip adds up for one person sharing a room, using the ranges above. Three nights in a simple Gangtok guesthouse come to about ₹4,500–8,000. Two nights in a Pelling guesthouse add ₹3,000–6,000, and two nights in a Yuksom homestay with dinner and breakfast add ₹3,000–5,600. Shared jeeps between the towns cost a few hundred rupees a leg, and a shared Tsomgo seat adds ₹800–1,500.

Lunches and snacks add another ₹250–500 a day. The total, before arrival costs, lands around ₹17,000–28,000. If you add a two-night shared North Sikkim package, add roughly ₹6,000–10,000 and one extra Gangtok night. A comfort version of the same week with a private car and good hotels costs several times as much, but it saves hours of waiting at jeep stands. Treat all of these as indicative for 2026, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to see Sikkim?
faqs.a: Use shared jeeps and homestays, base in two or three places, and join shared permit tours for Tsomgo and Lachung. Expect roughly ₹2,000–3,500 a day per person plus your arrival cost.

faqs.q: How much does a Gangtok to Lachung trip cost?
faqs.a: A shared two-night package can cost roughly ₹6,000–10,000 per person with homestay and meals, and a private jeep costs about ₹9,000–15,000 before rooms. Prices change by season; check current prices before you travel.

The Restricted Area Permit for foreigners is free, and most Protected Area Permits for Indian nationals are processed by agents as part of a package. Fees and rules change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Sikkim cheaper than Darjeeling or Bhutan?
faqs.a: Generally cheaper than Bhutan, whose visitors pay a daily fee, and similar to Darjeeling for budget stays. North Sikkim permit transport is the main extra cost.

faqs.q: How much cash should I carry?
faqs.a: Carry ₹10,000–15,000 in small notes into North Sikkim, where ATMs are few. Gangtok, Pelling and Jorethang have ATMs, but they can run out of cash during holidays.
January, February, July and August, when weather or road conditions keep visitors away. April–May and October–November are peak, and rates can rise 30–50 percent.
UPI works in Gangtok and many towns, but network is weak in the north. Carry cash for homestays, jeep seats and small shops.
Usually dinner and breakfast are included, which is why the nightly price per person looks higher than a bare room. Confirm when you book.

faqs.q: What does a day of food cost?
faqs.a: A budget day of momos, thukpa and thali costs roughly ₹500–900 per person, with homestay meals cheaper per plate. Hotel restaurants cost two to three times as much.
